title: The elephant, again
hookLine: each hand knows only a part of the elephant (Masnavi 3)
tomorrow: why would a chickpea try to jump out of the pot?

lines: NOBODY IN THE ROOM IS BLIND.
cards: Two screenshots of the same argument, cropped differently, posted by two people who are each completely sure.

You met the elephant in Rumi's Masnavi early on this path: people touch it in the dark, and each describes a different animal. Read it again and there's an odd detail. In Rumi's telling, nobody is blind.
The people can see perfectly well. The house is just dark. Why would Rumi set it up that way?
Why do people with working eyes all disagree?

teach.h: A PIPE, A FAN, A PILLAR, A THRONE.

teach.b: An elephant is kept in a dark house, and people who've never seen one go in to find out what it is. The hand on the trunk says: a water pipe. The hand on the ear: a fan.
On the leg: a pillar. On the back: a throne. Rumi didn't invent it.
In the Udana, a Buddhist text, a version has men blind from birth. Rumi changes one thing, and it solves the puzzle. If the people were blind, the fix would be new eyes, which nobody can hand out.
Since they can see, the problem isn't them. It's the light. Then comes his line: if each of them had held a candle, the difference would have gone out of their words.
Not one candle for the loudest person. A candle in each hand.
Rumi's readers hear the candle as the light of an inner sight, a light from God that sees the whole. But the shape of the puzzle works on an ordinary Tuesday too.
When two people who can both see are arguing about the same thing, the first question isn't who's blind.
It's how dark the room is, and what would bring more light: a question, a second source, the other person's full story.
Each hand is on something real.

how: Sufi teachers use the elephant in the dark house to teach humility about one's own grasp of the truth and the need for inner light; other versions of the story are told outside Islam too.

o: a vote that picks the most popular view
a louder voice that settles the argument
more light, so each part is seen in the whole

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.
p: the problem is light, not eyes
a telling with men blind from birth

s: in Rumi's telling, the people touching the elephant are blind
they can see. the house is dark. that's the detail that solves the puzzle.
Rumi says that with a candle, the difference would have gone out of their words
a candle in each hand, not one for the loudest.
the story means no one can ever know anything true
each hand is on something real, and light shows the whole. the elephant is real.

games.q: in history class, two classmates argue whether a leader was a hero or a villain. each quotes one true source. what's the candle here?
o: put both sources side by side, and look for what each one misses.
go with whoever argues louder, since they clearly know more.
decide nobody can know anything about the past, and drop it.
games.why: both can see; the room is dark. more light, not a louder hand, is what Rumi asks for.

practice: Choose one person whose view on something you only half know. Send them one open question about it, a real one, not a trap, and decide now that you'll read the whole answer before you reply.
Then set the phone face down and sit, letting your own argument rest.

wordCard.voice: The elephant: Rumi's story of sighted people touching an elephant in a dark house, and the candle that would end their quarrel.

orig.note: Persian and Arabic: candle; the light Rumi puts in each hand in the dark house.

carryVoice: Before the next argument: bring a candle, one for each hand in the room. Rumi's fifth story, three to go.
